newsitem.title: USA: Foot and mouth disease no threat to humans - USDA.
newsitem.headline: Foot and mouth disease no threat to humans - USDA.

text.p: The highly contagious foot and mouth disease, which has infected Taiwan's hog herd, is no threat to humans but is highly contagious among livestock and under some circumstances the virus can survive for up to a year, said a U.S. Department of Agriculture veterinarian.
"It is a viral disease and one of the most contagious diseases known to livestock," said Terry Wilson, a veterinary pathologist with the department's Animal and Plant Health Inspection Service.
Although not harmful to humans, humans can carry the virus from one livestock herd to another, he said.
Livestock at risk include cattle, hogs, goats and sheep. The disease can spread from one species to another.

Foot and mouth generally does not kill mature animals, but blisters that form on the mouths, tongues, feet, and udders of affected animals cause them to eat less. Milk production also declines in affected animals that are lactating.
"They don't eat and they become lame," Wilson said.
Depending on the strategy Taiwan uses, Wilson said it could take one to three years for that country to completely eradicate the disease.
Slaughtering the infected hogs may be the quickest method, he said, whereas trying to control the outbreak with vaccines would take longer.

Under certain temperature and wind conditions the virus can be spread up to 30 miles by wind currents. Plus, it can exist in meat and dairy products, livestock feed, and on veterinary equipment and the trucks that haul livestock. Also, if frozen, the virus can survive for up to a year.

Wilson said the virus can survive for up to a year at temperatures of four degrees Fahrenheit or less, eight to ten weeks at 22 degrees, 10 days at 37 degrees and about 30 minutes above 55 degrees, he said.
The last reported case in the United States was in 1929, but the virus was reported in Mexico in 1946, Wilson said.
